rules.rule: The separator set is EXACTLY these 37 codepoints (sorted, decimal/hex): 0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF, 0x0D CR, 0x20 SPACE, 0x21 !, 0x22 ", 0x23 #, 0x24 $, 0x25 %, 0x26 &, 0x27 ', 0x28 (, 0x29 ), 0x2A *, 0x2B +, 0x2C ,, 0x2D -, 0x2E ., 0x2F /, 0x3A :, 0x3B ;, 0x3C <, 0x3D =, 0x3E >, 0x3F ?, 0x40 @, 0x5B [, 0x5D ], 0x5E ^, 0x5F _, 0x60 `, 0x7B {, 0x7C |, 0x7D }, 0x7E ~. Nothing else. Equivalently: Python string.punctuation + string.whitespace MINUS backslash 0x5C.

UNDERSCORE 0x5F IS A SEPARATOR. This corrects the lead's fact list (which excluded only backslash). It is invisible to the single-char probe 'a'+C+'b' because both branches render as "a_b"; it is proven by the doubled probe: input 61 5f 5f 62 ("a__b") -> 61 5f 62 ("a_b"), and 5f5f5f ("___") -> 5f ("_").

BACKSLASH 0x5C is the ONLY ASCII punctuation character that is NOT a separator. It passes through verbatim and is never collapsed, even when directly adjacent to real separators: 61 5c 21 5c 62 ("a\\!\\b") -> 61 5c 5f 5c 62 ("a\\_\\b").

NO non-ASCII codepoint is a separator. Definitive NO: every codepoint from U+0001 to U+10FFFF excluding surrogates D800-DFFF (1,114,111 codepoints) was tested with the doubled probe 'a'+C+C+'b'; exactly 37 separators were found, all <= 0x7E. Zero parse anomalies, zero non-zero exits.

Specifically NOT separators (all measured, pass through byte-identical): U+00A0 NBSP, U+0085 NEL, U+1680 OGHAM SPACE MARK, U+180E, U+2000-U+200A all en/em/thin/hair spaces, U+200B ZWSP, U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR, U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE, U+FEFF BOM, all of U+2000-U+206F, U+2E00-U+2E7F, U+3000-U+303F, U+FF00-U+FF65 (fullwidth !, ", ., etc.), U+00A1-U+00FF, U+00B7 MIDDLE DOT, U+2014 EM DASH.

ASCII control characters other than 0x09-0x0D are NOT separators: 0x01-0x08, 0x0E-0x1F (including 0x1C-0x1F FS/GS/RS/US, which Python's str.split() treats as whitespace but string.whitespace does not), and 0x7F DEL. All pass through verbatim.
A run of MIXED different separators collapses to exactly ONE '_'. Measured: 61 21 20 09 0A 0D 0B 0C 2D 3B 2E 7E 5F 62 (a + 12 distinct separators + b) -> 61 5f 62 ("a_b").
A separator run at the very start and/or end is dropped entirely (no leading/trailing '_'). Measured: 21 21 21 5F 20 61 62 63 5F 21 21 21 -> 61 62 63 ("abc"); 20 09 0A 61 0D 0B 0C -> 61 ("a").

JS implementation: const SEP = /[\t\n\v\f\r !"#$%&'()*+,\-.\/:;<=>?@\[\]^_`{|}~]+/  (deliberately NO backslash in the class). slugify = s => { if (s === '') return ''; const parts = s.split(SEP).filter(p => p !== ''); return (parts.length ? parts.join('_') : '_').toLowerCase(); }  — note the all-separator case must yield '_' while empty input yields ''.

NUL 0x00 cannot be tested through this binary: argv strings are NUL-terminated by execve, and node's spawnSync rejects it (ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE 'must be a string without null bytes'). INFERRED not a separator, since Python's string.whitespace is ' \t\n\r\x0b\x0c' and string.punctuation contains no NUL.

INFERRED explanation for the backslash exclusion: the separator class is built by interpolating string.punctuation (which ends '...@[\\]^_`{|}~') raw into a regex character class, so the '\\]' pair is parsed as an escaped literal ']' and the backslash itself is consumed as the escape rather than becoming a class member. This predicts backslash is the only omission, which matches measurement exactly.

surprises: CORRECTION TO THE LEAD'S FACTS: underscore U+005F IS a separator. The lead's list said 'ASCII punctuation EXCEPT backslash' and separately implied only backslash was excluded — but the probe method the lead used ('a'+C+'b') is structurally blind to underscore, since a separator produces "a_b" and a literal underscore also produces "a_b". I re-ran the entire Unicode sweep with a doubled probe ('a'+C+C+'b'), which disambiguates, and underscore came back SEP. Direct proofs: 615f5f62 ('a__b') -> 615f62 ('a_b'), and 5f5f5f ('___') -> 5f ('_'). If underscore were not a separator those would be 'a__b' and '___'.

Practical consequence of the above: slugify collapses underscore runs already present in the input, so slugify is lossy on underscores and NOT a no-op on already-slugified text containing '__'. A naive JS implementation that omits '_' from the character class will differ on any input with repeated underscores or with an underscore adjacent to other punctuation ('a_!_b' -> 'a_b', measured 615f215f62 -> 615f62).

Backslash 0x5C really is the sole ASCII-punctuation exception, and its exclusion is total rather than contextual: it survives even when immediately flanked by separators ('a\\!\\b' -> 'a\\_\\b'). Almost certainly a latent bug in boltons where string.punctuation is interpolated raw into a regex character class and the '\\]' sequence eats the backslash as an escape.

Zero non-ASCII separators anywhere in Unicode. Every Unicode space and separator character is passed through untouched — NBSP, U+2000-U+200A, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE, U+1680 OGHAM SPACE MARK, and even U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR / U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR. So does the BOM U+FEFF and ZWSP U+200B, and every fullwidth punctuation mark in U+FF00-U+FF65. This means slugify output is NOT guaranteed to be free of whitespace-like characters.

0x1C-0x1F (FS/GS/RS/US) are NOT separators even though Python's bare str.split() treats them as whitespace — the implementation uses string.whitespace (6 chars), not str.split() semantics. 0x7F DEL and 0x85 NEL likewise not separators.

NUL 0x00 is fundamentally untestable through this binary: execve NUL-terminates argv, and node's spawnSync refuses the value outright with ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE. Marked INFERRED not-a-separator. A JS port must decide this on its own; string.punctuation and string.whitespace both exclude NUL, so exclude it.

The full sweep of all 1,114,111 non-surrogate codepoints ran with zero parse anomalies and zero non-zero exit codes — no codepoint caused an encoding error, crash, or unexpected output shape. Lone surrogates U+D800-U+DFFF could not be passed as arguments (not encodable to UTF-8) and were skipped.

rules.rule: PARSER SHAPE. Exactly two actions exist, in this registration order: (1) help — option strings ['-h','--help'], nargs=0; (2) a — option strings ['--a'], nargs=1 (single value), required=True, dest 'a', metavar 'A'. prefix_chars='-'. There are NO positional actions, so every token not consumed by an option becomes an "extra". Option-string matching is byte/case-exact: --A, --HELP, --hELP, -H, -a, -ax, -a=x are all NOT recognized.

PROG NAME. prog = basename of argv[0] of the process, not a hardcoded string. Invoked as /workspace/dataset/test4_executable it is "test4_executable"; through a symlink named zzz-name it is "zzz-name"; a copy named other_prog reports "other_prog".

EXIT CODES / STREAMS. Success -> stdout gets slugify(value)+"\n", stderr empty, exit 0. Help -> full help text on stdout, stderr empty, exit 0. Any parse error -> stdout EMPTY, stderr gets the usage block then the error line, exit 2. No other exit codes observed. Nothing is ever read from stdin (verified with stdin closed, with junk piped, and with "--a x\n" piped while argv was empty).

HELP TEXT (exact, 99 bytes, default 80-col env): "usage: test4_executable [-h] --a A

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
  --a A
". Header is "options:" (Python 3.10+ wording), one blank line after the usage line, two-space indent per entry, help text of -h starts at column 14 (2 spaces + "-h, --help" (10 chars) + 2 spaces), and "  --a A" has no help text and no trailing spaces. No trailing blank line.

ERROR BLOCK FORMAT (exact): stderr = "usage: " + <usage body, possibly wrapped> + "\n" + PROG + ": error: " + MESSAGE + "\n". Default env single-line form is "usage: test4_executable [-h] --a A". The MESSAGE is never wrapped, even at COLUMNS=20.

COLUMNS. Usage wrapping width = (int(COLUMNS) if COLUMNS is set and parses to a value > 0 else 80) - 2. So default width is 78. "usage: test4_executable [-h] --a A" (34 chars) stays on one line while COLUMNS>=36; at COLUMNS<=35 it becomes "usage: test4_executable [-h] --a\n                        A"; when "usage: "+prog exceeds the width the prog goes alone on line 1 and continuation lines are indented 7 spaces (len("usage: ")). COLUMNS="abc", "0", and "" all fall back to 80. COLUMNS also wraps the help body's description column. No other env var has any observed effect.

PHASE 1 — CLASSIFY EVERY TOKEN FIRST (left to right, before ANY action runs). Maintain seenDashDash=false. For token t at index i: (a) if !seenDashDash and t === "--": mark i as SEP and set seenDashDash=true; (b) else if seenDashDash: mark i as ARG; (c) else run classify(t) below -> either ARG or an option-tuple (marked OPT). Because this whole pass runs before consumption, an "ambiguous option" error raised here beats everything, including -h: argv ['-h','--=x'] exits 2 with the ambiguous error, help never prints.

classify(t) — exact ordered decision procedure. 1) t === "" -> ARG. 2) t[0] !== '-' -> ARG. 3) t is exactly '-h', '--help', or '--a' -> OPT(action, t, sep=null, explicitArg=null). 4) t.length === 1 (i.e. t === '-') -> ARG. 5) if t contains '=': name = part before the FIRST '=', rest = remainder; if name is exactly '-h', '--help', or '--a' -> OPT(action, name, sep='=', explicitArg=rest). 6) run getOptionTuples(t) (next rule); if it returns >1 tuple -> ERROR "ambiguous option: <t> could match <optionStrings joined by ', '>"; if exactly 1 -> OPT(that tuple). 7) NEGATIVE-NUMBER ESCAPE: if t matches Python regex ^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$ -> ARG (no registered option looks like a negative number, so this always wins). 8) if t contains a U+0020 SPACE -> ARG. 9) otherwise -> OPT(action=null, t, null, null)  (an UNKNOWN option; it will become an extra).

getOptionTuples(t) — abbreviation matcher. If t[0]==='-' AND t[1]==='-' (double dash): split off explicit arg at the first '=' if present (prefix = before '=', explicit = after; else prefix = t, explicit = null); then for each registered option string in registration order ['-h','--help','--a'], if optionString.startsWith(prefix) push (action, optionString, sep = (explicit!==null ? '=' : null), explicit). Note the direction: the REGISTERED name must start with the token prefix, so '--h'/'--he'/'--hel' resolve to --help, but '--aa', '--abc', '--A' match nothing. If t[0]==='-' and t[1]!=='-' (single dash): shortPrefix = t.slice(0,2), tail = t.slice(2); for each registered option string in order: if it EQUALS shortPrefix push (action, optionString, sep=null, explicitArg=tail); else if it startsWith(t) push (action, optionString, null, null).

ONLY ambiguity reachable: the token '--' with an '=' in it. '--=x' -> prefix '--' matches both '--help' and '--a' -> ERROR "ambiguous option: --=x could match --help, --a" (order = registration order, comma-space separated, and the reported token is the FULL original token including '=x'). A bare '--' can never trigger this because step (a) of phase 1 intercepts it.

NEGATIVE-NUMBER REGEX DETAIL (two gotchas). (i) Python's \d is UNICODE: any character in category Nd counts. So '-١' (Arabic-Indic), '-１' (fullwidth), '-२५' (Devanagari), '-1٢', '-.٥' are all accepted as values for --a. Category No/Nl do not count: '-¹1', '-①', '-Ⅳ' are treated as options and give "expected one argument". In JS use /^-[\p{Nd}]+$|^-[\p{Nd}]*\.[\p{Nd}]+$/u. (ii) Python's '$' also matches immediately before ONE trailing newline, so '-1
' and '-.5
' ARE accepted as values, while '-1

', '-1
x', and '-1' are not. Also accepted: '-0', '-05', '-12345678901234567890', '-0.0', '-.5', '-1.5'. Rejected (option-like): '-1e5', '-5x', '-5.', '-1_0', '-1,5', '-1.2.3', '-+1', '-1	2'.

PHASE 2 — CONSUME left to right from i=0. If token i is ARG or SEP, push the raw token onto extras and i+=1. If token i is OPT, run consumeOptional(i) which returns the next index. Actions are collected into a pending list inside consumeOptional and executed (in order) only when that call finishes; taking the help action prints help to stdout and exits 0 immediately; taking the 'a' action sets args.a = value, overwriting any previous value (LAST --a WINS: '--a x --a y' -> y; '--a x --a y --a z' -> z; '--a=x --a y' -> y; '--a x --a=y' -> y).

consumeOptional(i) with tuple (action, optionString, sep, explicitArg). If action === null (unknown option): push the raw token onto extras, return i+1. If explicitArg !== null: for the 'a' action (needs 1 value) the explicit arg IS the value -> pend (a, explicitArg), return i+1; for the 'help' action (needs 0 values): if sep === '=' OR explicitArg === '' OR explicitArg[0] is a prefix char ('-') -> ERROR "argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument <pythonRepr(explicitArg)>"; otherwise pend help, then retry with optionString = '-' + explicitArg[0] and remaining tail explicitArg.slice(1) (if that remainder starts with '=' set sep='=' and strip it; if it is empty set sep=explicitArg=null; else sep=''): if '-'+explicitArg[0] is registered loop again with that action, else push '-'+explicitArg onto extras and stop. If explicitArg === null: for 'help' pend help and return i+1; for 'a', require that index i+1 exists and is classified ARG -> value = token[i+1], return i+2, else ERROR "argument --a: expected one argument".

CONSEQUENCES of the short-option-tail rule (all measured): '-hx', '-ha', '-hh', '-hhx' and even the single token '-h y' all print help and exit 0 (for '-h y', getOptionTuples matches shortPrefix '-h' with tail ' y', so the "contains a space -> ARG" rule in classify step 8 is never reached). But '-h=x', '--h=x', '--help=x', '-hh=x' -> exit 2 "argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'"; '-h=', '--help=', '--h=' -> "... ignored explicit argument ''"; '-h-', '-h--', '-h-x', '-hh-x' -> "... ignored explicit argument '-'" / "'--'" / "'-x'" / "'-x'". Note the action name in that message is always the joined form "-h/--help".

pythonRepr(s) for the ignored-explicit message: normally single-quoted with backslash escaped as \\\\, newline as \\n, tab as \\t, CR as \\r; if s contains a single quote and no double quote, the whole thing is DOUBLE-quoted with the apostrophe left literal; if it contains both, single quotes are used and the apostrophe is escaped as \\'. Printable non-ASCII is kept literally (not \\u-escaped). Measured: 'dont'->'dont'; "don't"->"don't"; a'b\"c -> 'a\\'b\"c'; 'éü'->'éü'; literal backslash-n -> 'a\\\\nb'; real newline -> 'a\\nb'; tab -> '\\t'.

'--' SEPARATOR. The first '--' switches everything after it to plain ARG, so options after it are inert: ['--','-h'] and ['--','--a','x'] and ['--','--a=x'] all exit 2 with the required error (help does not fire, --a is not set). The '--' token itself is NOT removed and shows up verbatim in the unrecognized list, because no positional action ever consumes it: ['--a','x','--'] -> "unrecognized arguments: --"; ['--a','x','--','y'] -> "unrecognized arguments: -- y"; ['--a','x','--','--'] -> "unrecognized arguments: -- --"; ['--a','x','--','-h','--help'] -> "unrecognized arguments: -- -h --help". A '--' in the VALUE position is rejected: ['--a','--','x'] -> "argument --a: expected one argument" (optionals may not consume across '--').

PHASE 3 — POST-CHECKS, in this exact order. (1) if args.a was never set -> ERROR "the following arguments are required: --a" and exit 2. (2) else if extras is non-empty -> ERROR "unrecognized arguments: " + extras.join(' ') and exit 2. (3) else print slugify(args.a)+"\n", exit 0. The required error therefore ALWAYS beats the unrecognized error: ['-a','x'], ['x','--a'... no], ['p','q'], ['--b'], ['--b=1'], ['-z'], ['-xh'], ['--aa','x'], ['--abc=1'], ['--A','x'], ['--hELP'], ['-H'], [''], ['-'], ['--'] all report "the following arguments are required: --a".

UNRECOGNIZED-ARGUMENTS FORMAT. All extras are reported in ONE message, joined by a single U+0020, in original argv order (not sorted, not deduped), each token raw and unescaped (embedded newlines/tabs appear literally, an empty-string extra contributes nothing but its separator space is absent because join of ['']  is ''). Measured: ['--a','x','p','q'] -> "p q"; ['--a','x','q','p'] -> "q p"; ['p','--a','x','q'] -> "p q"; ['--b','x','--a','y'] -> "--b x"; ['--a','x','--b','y','--c'] -> "--b y --c"; ['--a=x','p\nq'] -> "p\nq" (real newline in stderr); ['--a','x',''] -> "unrecognized arguments: " with nothing after the space.

HELP SHORT-CIRCUIT ORDERING. -h/--help fires the moment it is CONSUMED, so it beats both post-checks but loses to any error raised earlier in the left-to-right consumption: ['-h'], ['-h','--a','x'], ['--a','x','-h'], ['--a','x','--help'], ['--help','--a'], ['--help','--b'], ['--b','--help'], ['-h','p','q'], ['-h','--h=y'], ['--h'], ['--he'], ['--hel'] -> help, exit 0. But ['--h=y','-h'] -> exit 2 ignored-explicit; ['--a','--help'] and ['--a','-x','-h'] -> exit 2 "argument --a: expected one argument"; ['-h','--=x'] -> exit 2 ambiguous (phase-1 error precedes everything).

'=' FORM DETAILS for --a. '--a=' -> value "" -> stdout is just "\n". '--a=x=y' -> value "x=y" (split at FIRST '=' only) -> "x_y". '--a==' -> value "=" -> "_". '--a=-x' -> value "-x" -> "x" (the equals form accepts dash-leading values with no restriction); '--a=--a' -> "a"; '--a=-' -> "_"; '--a=--' -> "_"; '--a=-h' -> "h". The space form '--a' '' also yields "\n". Only the exact names '-h','--help','--a' are recognized before '=' in classify step 5; '--h=x'/'--help=x' get there via the abbreviation matcher in step 6.

SPACE-FORM VALUE ACCEPTANCE for --a, i.e. which next token counts as a value: the token must classify as ARG. Accepted: anything not starting with '-'; '' (empty); '-' alone; any Unicode negative number per the regex rule; any dash-leading token containing a U+0020 space that is not matched by the abbreviation/short-prefix matcher (' -x', '-x ', '-x y', '-1 ', '--help y' -> value "--help y", '--h y', '--x y'); tokens starting with whitespace other than '-' ('\t-x'). Rejected (-> "argument --a: expected one argument"): '-x', '--a', '--a=y', '-h', '-h=1', '-x=1', '--h', '--help', '--1', '---', '--', '-1e5', '-5x', '-1_0', '-+1', '-\n', '-x\ty', '-1\t2', '-h y' (this one is matched as the -h short option instead and prints help).

A token consisting of '-' plus a single non-prefix char that is not 'h' (e.g. '-z', '-x') is an UNKNOWN option, not a positional, so it lands in extras rather than being usable as a value. '-zq' likewise. '-xh' is unknown ('-x' != '-h' and no registered name starts with '-xh').

'--a ' (trailing space) and '--a\t' are NOT the option --a: they fall through to classify step 8 (space) or step 9 (unknown option) and become extras, so ['--a ','x'] and ['--a\t','x'] exit 2 with the required error.

The runtime is Python 3.13-era argparse. The distinguishing evidence: '-hx' prints help and exits 0 (3.13 pushes the unmatched tail onto extras and still takes the -h action) while '-h=x' raises ignored-explicit — on Python <=3.12 BOTH raise "ignored explicit argument 'x'". Reimplementations targeting older argparse will get '-hx', '-ha', '-hh', '-hhx' and '-h y' wrong.

Only the FIRST '--' is treated as the separator; later '--' tokens are plain ARGs. This is INFERRED from the CPython algorithm — it is not observably distinguishable in this program because, with no positional actions defined, both the separator token and plain ARGs end up in extras identically (['--a','x','--','--'] -> "-- --" either way).

surprises: THE ONE REAL DEFECT: the prior report's COLUMNS rule is wrong whenever stdout is a TTY. It claims the width falls back to a constant 80 when COLUMNS is unset/unparseable/<=0. In fact CPython's shutil.get_terminal_size() then queries the terminal attached to sys.__stdout__, so on a 30-column pty the usage wraps even with COLUMNS unset, COLUMNS=0, COLUMNS=abc or COLUMNS=-5. 80 is only the fallback when stdout is not a terminal. A reimplementation that hardcodes 80 will produce wrong output for interactive users.

The wrap width comes from STDOUT even though the usage block for errors goes to STDERR. Redirecting stdout to a file while leaving stderr on a 30-col tty gives unwrapped 80-col usage on stderr; the reverse redirection gives wrapped usage on stderr.

argv bytes that are not valid UTF-8 are decoded with errors='replace', not surrogateescape: each bad byte becomes U+FFFD (EF BF BD) and the program never fails (exit 0). C0 AF yields TWO U+FFFD and ED A0 80 yields THREE. The prior report did not test non-UTF-8 argv at all.

The 'ignored explicit argument' repr escapes non-printable characters, which the prior report missed entirely: U+00A0 -> \xa0, U+00AD -> \xad, U+0085 -> \x85, U+007F -> \x7f, U+200B -> ​, U+E0001 -> \U000e0001. Combining marks, U+FFFD and emoji stay literal. The dividing line is Python's str.isprintable().
The 'contains a space' escape hatch is U+0020 only: '-1<NBSP>' and '-1<U+2028>' are rejected as values for --a while '-1 ' is accepted. A JS implementation using /\s/ would be wrong.

'--a=--=x' parses cleanly to the value '--=x' (exit 0) even though the bare token '--=x' is an ambiguous-option error - the exact-name-before-first-'=' check short-circuits before the ambiguity matcher.
